facts.fact: Described in 2023 by Luiz F. C. Tencatt, Steven Grant and Rebecca F. Bentley in Neotropical Ichthyology as a new color-changing Corydoras.
The species name comes from the Ancient Greek kolossós, meaning a large or giant statue, and refers to its large, robust, armoured body.
The holotype measures 44.5 mm SL and was collected in 2022 in the rio Jutaí near where it meets the rio Solimões.
The species can be told apart by a mosaic of coalescent platelets that covers most of the underside of the trunk.
It has a large, arched, dark brown to black mask-like patch that runs across the eye from the interopercle to the top of the head.
The caudal fin has no dark transverse blotches, and the flanks have no rows of dark blotches.
There is a conspicuous dark patch on the front of the dorsal fin.
It can switch between a light phase (tan to light brown, with clear fins) and a dark phase (partly or fully black); the change may be influenced by substrate, light and water colour.
The describers suggest the black phase may serve as a warning (aposematic) signal, but this has not been tested.
The describers assessed it as Least Concern under IUCN criteria.
Aquarists knew it as CW045 before its description, and it was renamed the Colossus Corydoras after being described in 2023.
It has a tall body, a dark grey body, a black band across the eye, an orange patch on top of the head, and a longer dorsal fin than most corydoras.
Unlike Corydoras armatus, it has a bright orange-yellow spot on the neck and gill covers.
It is now placed in the genus Hoplisoma, as Hoplisoma colossus.
The dorsal and pectoral fin spines are linked to venom glands, and a sting can be very painful.
It is known only from its type locality, the rio Jutaí, a tributary in the Amazon basin in Amazonas State, Brazil.
The video says it is endemic to the Amazon river and its tributaries near Jutaí, Brazil.
The rio Jutaí is a blackwater river with transitional water chemistry (mean pH about 5.96) and very low conductivity.
The riverbed is mostly white sand with leaf litter and wood, and there are few aquatic plants.
In the wild it lives alongside Corydoras sp. CW116 and CW117.
It is fairly common in the aquarium trade but sold in small numbers, under the code CW045 and the names 'Lessex' (light phase) and 'Resex' (dark phase).
Part of the rio Jutaí lies within two conservation units.
It is uncommon in the hobby and fairly expensive.
Its high price and sensitivity to poor water make it unsuitable for beginners.
Aquarium Glaser first imported it from the Rio Jutaí in 2009 under the name Corydoras sp. aff. armatus.
Keep it in a group of at least six; otherwise the fish may become withdrawn and stressed.
Fine sand is the best substrate, though smooth gravel can also be used. Add cover such as driftwood, rocks, or tall or floating plants.
It prefers soft water but is flexible, as long as sudden changes in water parameters are avoided.
It adapts well to different water conditions, but shows its best colours in natural-like conditions.
It is a scavenging omnivore that takes sinking foods such as wafers, pellets and granules, as well as small live, frozen and freeze-dried foods such as bloodworm and daphnia.
Do not expect it to survive on leftover food alone.
It readily accepts granular foods, tablet food and frozen bloodworm.
It is peaceful and sociable, and suits community tanks with small, peaceful fish, shrimp and snails. Avoid much larger or aggressive fish.
It is peaceful toward its own kind and toward other fish species, and should be kept in groups.
Males have a somewhat tubular genital papilla.
In some mature fish of both sexes, the first (and sometimes the second) dorsal-fin ray is greatly extended.
Females grow larger and are rounder and broader-bodied than males when mature.
Males reach about 5.5 cm and females about 6.0 cm.
In aquaria, Hans-Georg Evers has bred it and documented the young growing from 9.0 to 28.0 mm.

The video says there were no breeding reports when it was made, and suggests the usual corydoras method: a separate tank, conditioning with live and frozen food, and cooler water changes to trigger spawning.
The video expects eggs to be laid on leaves or glass with no parental care, to hatch in 2 to 4 days, and the fry to be fed infusoria or microworms.
For breeding, it is recommended to keep the species in a species-only tank.

care.quote: The water temperature can be between 24 and 30°C.
